claims.text: The corrosion resistance of high-alloy steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily governed by the characteristics of their native passivating oxide film.
Chromium enrichment of the passive film improves corrosion resistance.
A continuous passive film with low defect density provides greater protection than a cracked, porous, or discontinuous film.
Passive-film chromium content, continuity, and defect density control ionic transport and metal dissolution under operational stresses.
Controlled oxidation treatments can alter passive-film chromium content, thickness, and defect density while leaving the steel's bulk composition constant.
A dense, continuous, chromium-enriched oxide layer acts as a physical and chemical barrier protecting the substrate.
The chromium-enriched oxide barrier suppresses ionic migration and metal dissolution.
Increasing passive-film chromium content and reducing its defect density reduces the corrosion rate.
Degradation of the passive film increases corrosion susceptibility by enabling greater ionic transport.
Samples with enhanced passive films will have lower corrosion rates than samples retaining the baseline native film.
Samples with enhanced passive films will exhibit higher polarization resistance than baseline samples.
Samples with enhanced passive films will exhibit more positive pitting potentials than baseline samples.
Samples with deliberately compromised passive films will exhibit increased corrosion rates relative to samples with enhanced films and may meet or exceed baseline corrosion rates.
The proposed passive-film mechanism should operate in acidic or basic chemical-processing environments at elevated temperature and pressure.
The proposed passive-film mechanism should operate in high-temperature water under moderate radiation flux representative of nuclear-power conditions.
The hypothesis is not intended to cover conditions that completely remove the oxide film or introduce dominant corrosion mechanisms such as extreme abrasion or highly aggressive chemistry.
The quantitative effects of film defect density and thickness under simultaneous thermal, chemical, and radiation stresses are not well defined.

A lack of any statistically significant corrosion-current, polarization-resistance, or pitting-potential difference between both modified groups and the untreated baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
